trigger: concurrency + cross-plugin checkout + new CI write-permissions

doubts.claim_under_doubt: the added `git ls-remote` stale-run guard, combined with the workflow's `concurrency: cancel-in-progress` group, makes the older-run-overwrites-newer-run race 'almost fully closed'
doubts.disproof_attempt: The guard only re-validates that `main`'s tip still equals `$GITHUB_SHA` at check time — it does not exclusively lock the `bot/traceability-regen` branch across the gap between that check and the actual `git push --force` several shell lines later (auth, config, checkout, add, commit, push). Concrete interleaving that defeats it: run A (older push SHA1) reaches the ls-remote check while `main` is still at SHA1 -> check passes legitimately. Before A's `git push --force` lands, a second, unrelated merge advances `main` to SHA2, triggering run B, whose own ls-remote check (against the now-current SHA2) also passes legitimately. Both checks were individually correct at the instant they ran; the race is now purely which run's `git push --force` to `bot/traceability-regen` lands LAST on GitHub's server, which is a function of network/runner-scheduling latency, not of check order. If A's slower push lands after B's, A's SHA1-based (older) regen silently clobbers B's SHA2-based (fresher) one, with no further check to catch it — exactly the failure the guard exists to prevent, just moved one layer down. `cancel-in-progress` narrows but doesn't close this: it cancels the WORKFLOW, but the comment in ci.yml itself admits cancellation 'is not instantaneous' and a run already past the check can 'still finish'. This project's own documented workflow (parallel iterates merging to main) makes two main-pushes landing within the same multi-minute job window plausible, not a remote edge case.
doubts.what_would_resolve_it: Either (a) a written rebuttal accepting the residual risk explicitly — worst case is a briefly-stale regen on a PR that a human reviews before merge, and the NEXT push-to-main drift cycle self-heals it, so no unrecoverable state — or (b) close the gap for real with a second, job-scoped `concurrency: group: traceability-regen-pr / cancel-in-progress: false` so overlapping regen-PR pushes literally cannot execute concurrently, rather than relying on a narrowed-but-nonzero TOCTOU window.

doubts.claim_under_doubt: job-scoped `permissions: {contents: write, pull-requests: write}` is safe alongside checking out and dynamically importing code from a second, pinned repo into the same job
doubts.disproof_attempt: `build_manifest`, `_validate_manifest`, and `_test_links_io` from `.ci-shipwright-compliance` are executed as live Python inside the `Regenerate + diff` step, in the SAME job/process that later runs `gh auth setup-git` + `git push --force` with the write-scoped `GH_TOKEN` (`Open a regen PR` step). Nothing sandboxes the earlier step from the later one within a single job: any code reachable from that import graph can write to the files `$GITHUB_ENV`/`$GITHUB_PATH` point at (both are ordinary env vars visible to any subprocess in the step) to inject env vars or prepend a malicious directory to `PATH` for every SUBSEQUENT step — including the one that authenticates `git`/`gh` with write credentials. That is the standard 'poisoned pipeline execution' pattern GitHub Actions security guidance calls out, and this job's architecture doesn't defend against it: least-privilege here is scoped to WHICH repo the token can touch, not to WHEN in the job's lifetime untrusted-relative-to-this-repo code gets to run before the token is used. The ADR's credential-risk discussion only reasons about 'don't provision a NEW PAT' — it doesn't address this exposure window for the EXISTING default token.
doubts.what_would_resolve_it: Either a reasoned rebuttal — the pinned checkout is same-org code reviewed via this org's own PR process (comparable trust to first-party), and GitHub branch-protection on `main` independently blocks a direct malicious push regardless of token misuse (worth explicitly confirming the ruleset has no bypass actor for Actions/admin) — or split into two jobs: a read-only job computes the regen and uploads it as an artifact, a second job (`needs:`, holding the write permissions) downloads the artifact and does only `git`/`gh` operations, never importing the pinned code itself.

doubts.claim_under_doubt: the auto-opened PR is a safe, inspectable staging point before a human merges
doubts.disproof_attempt: The push to `bot/traceability-regen` uses `git push --force` (not `--force-with-lease`), and the job re-runs on EVERY subsequent push to `main` while this PR remains unmerged — and will keep finding drift (since `main` stays stale by definition until this exact PR merges), so it will force-push again on virtually every unrelated merge in the interim. This silently destroys ANY commit a human added to that branch out-of-band in the meantime — including the PR body's own suggested nudge ('e.g. an empty commit re-triggers the required checks'), and any hand-fix a reviewer might push instead of just merging. Not flagged in the ADR's 'Consequences' section, which discusses a maintainer CLOSING the PR but not a maintainer PUSHING to it.
doubts.what_would_resolve_it: Switch to `--force-with-lease` so a human's intervening commit at least causes a visible push failure instead of silent loss, and/or note in the PR body that the branch is bot-owned and any manual commit will be overwritten on the next drift cycle.

summary: 3 doubts (2 medium, 1 low) across concurrency/ordering, boundary & contract, and reversibility. Attempted disproof on all four lenses; hidden-coupling/blast-radius (the derived-snapshot F11 rule, PR-review sensitive-path tiering) checked and did not turn up a defect — F11's derived-snapshot gate is not wired into this repo's CI at all (verified: only referenced in comments/planning docs, never invoked in .github/workflows), so it cannot block the bot PR, and the manifest file is not in the PR-review sensitive-path set. The $GITHUB_SHA-injection angle specifically requested by the launcher did not pan out: GITHUB_SHA is always an opaque 40-hex commit SHA on this job's triggers (push/workflow_dispatch, pull_request excluded), never attacker-influenced text, so the shell body's use of it is safe. None of the three findings rise to a blocking severity given the advisory framing and the human-gated merge step, but the implementer should address each in writing rather than let 'advisory + not auto-merged' stand in as an implicit answer to all three.
